title: Problem Overview
content: Erdős Problem 848 asks for the maximum size of A ⊆ {1,...,N} such that ab + 1 is never squarefree for all a, b ∈ A. Solved by Sawhney: the answer is ⌊N/25⌋ for large N.
mathContext: The problem sits at the intersection of extremal combinatorics and multiplicative number theory. The non-squarefreeness constraint ab + 1 ≡ 0 (mod p²) for some prime p forces elements of A into specific residue classes. The extremal sets are arithmetic progressions mod 25, arising from 5² | ab + 1 when a ≡ b ≡ 7 or 18 (mod 25).

title: Imports and Namespace Setup
content: Imports Mathlib.Tactic for general proof automation, Mathlib.Data.Nat.Basic for natural number operations, and Mathlib.Data.Nat.Prime.Basic for the `Nat.Prime` predicate used in the squarefree definition.
mathContext: The formalization needs only basic natural number infrastructure: primality testing ($p.\text{Prime}$), divisibility ($\mid$), and modular arithmetic ($\%$). No advanced Mathlib modules (e.g., Finset cardinality bounds or analytic number theory) are required because the deep results are axiomatized.

title: Squarefree Definition
content: **`IsSquarefree n`** holds when no prime squared divides n. Equivalently, in the prime factorization n = Π p^{aₚ}, all exponents aₚ are 0 or 1.
mathContext: The density of squarefree numbers is $6/\pi^2 \approx 0.608$, proved via inclusion-exclusion over prime squares: $\prod_p (1 - 1/p^2) = 1/\zeta(2) = 6/\pi^2$. Most numbers are squarefree, so requiring $ab + 1$ to be non-squarefree is a non-trivial constraint.

title: Non-Squarefree Product Property and Extremal Function
content: **`HasNonSqfreeProductProp A`** requires that for ALL pairs a, b ∈ A (including a = b), the product ab + 1 is not squarefree. **`maxNonSqfreeSet N`** is axiomatized as the maximum cardinality of such a set in {1,...,N}, with the trivial upper bound maxNonSqfreeSet(N) ≤ N.
mathContext: The 'including $a = b$' part means $a^2 + 1$ must also be non-squarefree for every $a \in A$. Since $a^2 + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$ has exactly 2 solutions mod $p^2$ for primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ (by Hensel's lemma lifting from the 2 roots of $x^2 \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$) and 0 solutions for $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, this constrains $A$ to unions of specific residue classes modulo prime squares.

title: Mod 25 Construction (Lower Bound)
content: The set {n ≡ 7 (mod 25)} satisfies the property: for a ≡ b ≡ 7 (mod 25), ab + 1 ≡ 49 + 1 = 50 ≡ 0 (mod 25), so 5² | ab + 1. This gives |A| = ⌊N/25⌋, establishing the lower bound.
mathContext: The residue 7 mod 25 satisfies $7^2 + 1 = 50 = 2 \cdot 25$, so $25 \mid a^2 + 1$ for all $a \equiv 7 \pmod{25}$. Similarly $18^2 + 1 = 325 = 13 \cdot 25$. The symmetry $7 + 18 = 25$ reflects the two square roots of $-1$ modulo $25$: since $5 \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$, the equation $x^2 \equiv -1 \pmod{5}$ has solutions $x \equiv \pm 2 \pmod{5}$, which lift to $x \equiv 7, 18 \pmod{25}$ via Hensel's lemma.

title: Van Doorn's Upper Bound
content: Van Doorn showed |A|/N ≤ 2·Σ_{p≡1(4)} 1/p² ≈ 0.108. The formalization encodes this as maxNonSqfreeSet(N) · 1000 ≤ 108 · N + C for some constant C.
mathContext: The factor 2 comes from $a^2 + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}$ having exactly 2 solutions for primes $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. The sum $\sum_{p \equiv 1(4)} 1/p^2$ converges rapidly: $1/5^2 + 1/13^2 + 1/17^2 + 1/29^2 + \cdots \approx 0.054$, giving the bound $\sim 0.108$. The integer encoding $1000 \cdot |A| \leq 108 \cdot N + C$ avoids rational arithmetic in the formalization.

title: Sawhney's Exact Solution
content: **Sawhney's theorem**: For all sufficiently large N, maxNonSqfreeSet(N) = ⌊N/25⌋. The extremal construction is tight, closing the gap between the N/25 lower bound and the 0.108N upper bound.
mathContext: This closes the gap between the $N/25 = 0.04N$ lower bound and Van Doorn's $0.108N$ upper bound. The proof that the lower bound is tight uses modern tools from additive combinatorics, particularly the structure theory of dense subsets of residue classes and the interplay between multiplicative characters modulo prime squares.

title: Structural Characterization of Extremal Sets
content: Any extremal set of size ⌊N/25⌋ for large N must consist entirely of elements ≡ 7 (mod 25) or entirely of elements ≡ 18 (mod 25). No mixing of residue classes is possible, and no other residue class achieves the maximum.
mathContext: This uniqueness result (up to the $7 \leftrightarrow 18$ symmetry) is a stability theorem: not only is $\lfloor N/25 \rfloor$ the maximum, but any set achieving it is structurally rigid. This parallels Turán-type stability results in extremal graph theory, where near-extremal configurations must resemble the extremal one. The two classes correspond to the two roots of $x^2 \equiv -1 \pmod{25}$, reflecting a $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ symmetry group.
